documentation.title: Oblique frictional impact between two free deformable bodies, 3D
documentation.description:
The 3D counterpart of ContactImpactOblique2d. A deformable SPHERE strikes a deformable SLAB obliquely, with Coulomb friction, under large sliding. Nothing is fixed anywhere: both bodies are free, the only force is the contact traction, and the sphere slides while the patch forms, grows and travels.
TWO INDEPENDENT INVARIANTS, which is what makes the 3D run worth its cost:
1. COULOMB. sqrt(contactForceX^2 + contactForceY^2) / contactForceZ = mu while every point slips. The primary surface is the slab's FLAT top, so the normal is exactly (0,0,1) in every configuration and the resultant splits without ambiguity into normal (Z) and tangential (X,Y). 2. SYMMETRY. contactForceY must VANISH: the launch velocity has no y component and the geometry is mirror-symmetric about the xz-plane -- now WITH FRICTION ACTING, which the frictionless ContactImpactSphere3d cannot test. A mispaired point, a normal from the wrong facet, or a friction direction built in the wrong frame breaks it immediately. It is also the invariant a 2D model cannot provide at all: in 2D the tangent plane is one-dimensional and the friction direction has no freedom to go wrong; in 3D it has two, and this pins them.
WHY SPHERE-ON-SLAB. On an oblique sphere-on-sphere impact the contact normal rotates during contact and no reported quantity gives the Coulomb ratio. Meeting a plane buys the exact force split at no cost to the striker: the sphere is still doubly curved and genuinely faceted, and it is the SECONDARY surface, so its curvature is exercised on the side where it is hard.
RESOLUTION is coarse deliberately and weakens neither invariant, because both hold POINTWISE at every slipping point. What the coarse mesh costs is the pressure DISTRIBUTION, which is not asserted. tangent="consistent" because every point slips and nothing sticks.
